title: A Differential Geometric View and Explainability of GNN on Evolving Graphs
authors: Yazheng Liu, Xi Zhang, Sihong Xie
text:
Graph neural networks (GNN) are now the state-of-the-art method for graph representation in many applications, such as social network modeling [1] and molecule property prediction [2], pose estimation in computer vision [3], smart cities [4], fraud detection [5], and recommendation systems [6]. A GNN outputs a probability distribution \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G;\bm{\theta}) of Y, the class random variable of a node (node classification), a link (link prediction), or a graph (graph classification), using trained parameters \bm{\theta}. Graphs can be evolving, with edges/nodes added and removed. For example, social networks are undergoing constant updates [7]; graphs representing chemical compounds are constantly tweaked and tested during molecule design. In a sequence of graph snapshots, without loss of generality, let G_{0}\to G_{1} be any two snapshots where the source graph G_{0} evolves to the destination graph G_{1}. \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{0};\bm{\theta}) will evolve to \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{1};\bm{\theta}) accordingly, and we aim to model and explain the evolution of \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G;\bm{\theta}) with respect to G_{0}\to G_{1} to help humans understand the evolution [8,9,10,11,12]. For example, a GNN’s prediction of whether a chemical compound is promising for a target disease during compound design can change as the compound is fine-tuned, and it is useful for the designers to understand how the GNN’s prediction evolves with respect to compound perturbations.

To model graph evolution, existing work [13,14] analyzed the macroscopic change in graph properties, such as graph diameter, density, and power law, but did not analyze how a parametric model responses to graph evolution. Recent work [15,16,17,18,7] investigated learning a model for each graph snapshot and thus the model is evolving, while we focus on modeling a fixed GNN model over evolving graphs. A more fundamental drawback of the above work is the discrete viewpoint of graph evolution, as individual edges and nodes are added or deleted. Such discrete modeling fails to describe the corresponding change in \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G;\bm{\theta}), which is generated by a computation graph that can be perturbed with infinitesimal amount and can be understood as a sufficiently smooth function. The smoothness can help identify subtle infinitesimal changes contributing significantly to change in \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G;\bm{\theta}), and thus more faithfully explain the change.

Regarding explaining GNN predictions, there is promising progress made with static graphs, including local or global explanation methods [19]. Local methods explain individual GNN predictions by selecting salient subgraphs [8], nodes, or edges [9]. Global methods [20,21] optimize simpler surrogate models to approximate the target GNN and generate explaining models or graph instances. Existing counterfactual or perturbation-based methods [22] attribute a static prediction to individual edges or nodes by optimizing a perturbation to the input graph to maximally alter the target prediction, thus giving a sense of explaining graph evolution. However, the perturbed graph found by these algorithms can differ from G_{0}, and thus does not explain the change from \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{0};\bm{\theta}) to \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{1};\bm{\theta}). Both prior methods DeepLIFT [23] and GNN-LRP [9] can find propagation paths that contribute to prediction changes. However, they have a fixed G_{0} for any G_{1} and thus fail to model smooth evolution between arbitrary G_{0} and G_{1}. They also handle multiple classes independently [9] or uses the log-odd of two predicted classes Y=j and Y=j^{\prime} to measure the changes in \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G;\bm{\theta}) [23], rather than the overall divergence between two distributions.

To facilitate smooth evolution from \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{0};\bm{\theta}) to \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{1};\bm{\theta}) (we ignore the fixed \bm{\theta} in the sequel), in Section 3.1, we set up a coordinate system for \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G) using the contributions of paths on the computation graphs to \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G) relative to a global reference graph. We rewrite the distribution \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G) for node classification, link prediction, and graph classification using these coordinates, so that \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G) for any graph G is embedded in this Euclidean space spanned by the paths. For classification, the distributions \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G) have only c-1 sufficient statistics and form an intrinsic low-dimensional manifold embedded in the constructed extrinsic embedding Euclidean space. In Section 3.2, we study the curvature of the manifold local to a particular \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G). We derive the Fisher information matrix I of \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G) with respect to the path coordinates. As the KL-divergence between \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{0}) and \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{1}) that are sufficiently close can be approximated by a quadratic function with the Fisher information matrix, \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G) does not necessarily evolve linearly in the extrinsic coordinates but adapts to the curved intrinsic geometry of the manifold around \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G). Previous explanation methods [23,9] taking a linear view point will not sufficiently model such curved geometry. Our results justify KL-divergence as a faithfulness metric of explanations adopted in the literature. The manifold allows a set of curves \gamma(s) with the continuous time variable s\in[0,1] to model differentiable evolution between two distributions. With a novel reparameterization, we devise a convex optimization problem to optimally select a curve depending on a small number of extrinsic coordinates to approximate the evolution of \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{0}) into \mathsf{Pr}(Y|G_{1}) following the local manifold curvature. Empirically, in Section 4, we show that the proposed model and algorithm help select sparse and salient graph elements to concisely and faithfully explain the GNN responses to evolving graphs on 8 graph datasets with node classification, link prediction, and graph classification, with edge additions and/or deletions.
